verdict.definition: The evidence in the paper, read with the cited and established literature, establishes the claim as written.
The claim holds only in a narrower or weaker form than written. The review states exactly which narrower statement is established.
The evidence offered does not establish the claim. The claim may still be true; it has not been shown.
The paper's own data, or an outside source the reviewer opened, is inconsistent with the claim.
The claim cannot be judged from the material available, for example because its evidence is in supplementary material that was not supplied.

severity.definition: A headline claim of the paper does not stand if this claim fails.
A substantial conclusion changes if this claim fails, but the headline could survive in a narrower form.
A supporting detail changes if this claim fails; no conclusion does.
An error of wording, labelling, formatting or citation form that affects no conclusion.

confidence.definition: The verdict rests on evidence the reviewer read directly (the paper's own data and, for outside sources, their full text) and on reasoning an expert would be unlikely to dispute.
The verdict rests partly on abstracts or secondary sources, or on a judgement that experts might weigh differently.
The verdict rests on limited access to the evidence or on recollection of the field. Treat it as a flag for an expert to check.

tier.name: Routine
tier.definition: Standard methods or values, consistent with established knowledge. Ordinary evidence is enough.

tier.name: Substantial
tier.definition: A new result within an established framework. Needs the evidence a careful paper in the field would show.

tier.name: Exceptional
tier.definition: Would change accepted understanding, or exceeds established benchmarks by a wide margin. Needs evidence strong enough to exclude ordinary explanations.

claim_type.definition: Something the paper reports seeing or measuring.
A numerical value, with or without an uncertainty, that the paper extracts or derives from data.
A statement about how something was done, or how well an instrument or procedure performs.
A result obtained from a model, derivation, calculation or simulation.
What an observation, value or model result is said to mean, show or be caused by.
A statement the paper takes from another work.
A statement that a result agrees with, exceeds or differs from another result, model or benchmark.
A statement about the novelty, importance or implications of the work.

access.definition: The full text was opened and read in this run.
Only the abstract or a publisher summary was read in this run.
Only the bibliographic record was confirmed.
The source could not be reached.

citation_status.definition: The source was opened and supports the statement it is cited for.
The citation or the statement was wrong and has been fixed; the source as now cited supports the statement as now written.
The citation was dropped from the review.
The source was not opened beyond its bibliographic record, or was not reached at all.

citation_error.definition: The source exists, but the authors, title, venue, year or identifier given for it were wrong.
The source exists and was cited correctly, but does not say what the review attributed to it.
No such work could be found.
Another error, described in the note.

citation_verdict.definition: The source reports what the paper cites it for.
The source supports a narrower statement, or the same statement in a different system or regime.
The source does not contain what the paper cites it for.
The source reports the opposite, or a null result, for what the paper cites it for.
The source could not be read well enough to judge.

verification.definition: Every outside source the review relies on was opened and is confirmed or corrected.
Some outside sources the review relies on remain unverified.
No outside source was verified, for example because the tool had no web access.

rules: Use the exact words of this rubric. A value that is not listed here is invalid.
One verdict per claim. If part of a claim holds and part does not, split the claim in the registry and judge the parts separately.
Severity is the consequence for the paper's headline if the claim fails. It is empty when the verdict is Supported.
A headline claim that does not stand is itself Critical. If a narrower form of it stands, it is Major.
A claim that fails only because a claim it depends on fails lists that claim under blocked-by.
Contradicted, or a severity of Critical, requires a basis anyone can check: a location in the paper, or a citation whose source was opened in this run.
A statement too vague to test is Unsupported, and its block says what would make it testable. Plausibility is recorded in the reasoning and the confidence, not in the verdict.
A missing optional control is a note, not a reason to lower a verdict.
Tier describes how much evidence a claim needs. It is not a judgement of whether the claim is right.
